skill.name: security-audit
skill.description: Review security of command execution, tool permissions, and API key handling. Use when user mentions "security review", "audit", "check security", "vulnerabilities", or before deploying to production.
skill.summary: Read-only security review checklist for command execution, tool permissions, secrets, WebSockets, and frontend risks.
skill.author: AppleLamps

security_audit.summary: The reviewed skill is a read-only security audit checklist. All static findings are false positives caused by Markdown inline code references to files, functions, environment files, and security topics rather than executable behavior.

finding_verdicts.reason: Line 10 uses Markdown inline code to name backend/main.py as an audit target. It does not execute a command or instruct shell execution.
Line 11 references run_terminal_command() as a function to review for shell injection. The text directs analysis of risk and does not invoke the function.
Line 16 lists allowed tool names inside Markdown backticks. The backticks are formatting only and do not create a command execution path.
Line 21 references .env as a file that should be ignored by version control. This is a protective checklist item, not shell execution.
Line 23 mentions python-dotenv as a dependency to verify during a secrets review. It is descriptive Markdown text and does not run an external command.
Line 26 names the /ws endpoint as an audit target using inline code formatting. It does not execute a command or initiate network activity.
Line 23 asks the auditor to verify environment-variable handling through python-dotenv. The skill does not read environment variables or request secret values.
Line 21 instructs users to confirm .env is in .gitignore. This reduces accidental secret exposure and does not access or reveal the file contents.

content.value_statement: Security gaps in command execution, secrets, and WebSockets can reach production unnoticed. This skill guides Claude, Codex, or Claude Code through a read-only review.
actual_capabilities: Reviews command execution paths for shell injection and missing timeouts.
Checks declared tool permissions for chat and agent mode restrictions.
Guides review of environment files, hardcoded API keys, and dotenv usage.
Covers WebSocket authentication, message validation, and user input injection points.
Prompts frontend checks for markdown rendering, image uploads, and client-side secrets.
Organizes audit output into critical issues, warnings, and recommendations.
limitations: Does not modify files or apply fixes without separate user approval.
Depends on the files and context available to the AI assistant.
Does not run exploit payloads or dynamic penetration tests.
Targets web applications with patterns similar to the referenced project structure.

use_cases.title: Pre-Release Security Check
use_cases.description: Review command execution, secrets, WebSockets, and frontend handling before a deployment.

use_cases.title: AI Tool Permission Review
use_cases.description: Verify that chat and agent modes expose only the tools required for safe operation.

use_cases.title: Focused Codebase Triage
use_cases.description: Produce a clear list of critical issues, warnings, and recommendations for a web terminal project.

prompt_templates.title: Run Basic Audit
prompt_templates.scenario: Beginner review before sharing a project.
prompt_templates.prompt: Run a read-only security audit of this project. Focus on command execution, secrets, WebSockets, and frontend risks.

prompt_templates.title: Check Deployment Readiness
prompt_templates.prompt: Review this codebase for security issues that should block production deployment. Separate critical issues, warnings, and recommendations.

prompt_templates.title: Audit Tool Permissions
prompt_templates.prompt: Audit the chat and agent tool permissions. Confirm whether each mode exposes only the required tools and note bypass risks.

prompt_templates.title: Perform Targeted Risk Review
prompt_templates.prompt: Perform a targeted read-only review of command execution, environment variable handling, WebSocket authentication, input validation, markdown rendering, and uploads.

output_examples.input: Run a security audit before deploy.
output_examples.output: A structured report with critical issues, warnings, and recommendations covering command execution, secrets, WebSockets, and frontend handling.

output_examples.input: Check whether chat mode permissions are safe.
output_examples.output: A permission review that lists allowed tools, notes unexpected access, and explains any bypass or escalation risk.

output_examples.input: Review API key handling in this project.
output_examples.output: A secrets-management assessment that flags hardcoded keys, missing ignore rules, unsafe logging, and environment variable misuse.

best_practices: Run the audit with read-only access unless the user explicitly approves fixes.
Review findings against the actual code before treating them as confirmed vulnerabilities.
Prioritize command injection, exposed secrets, and unauthenticated WebSocket access first.
anti_patterns: Do not ask the assistant to exploit vulnerabilities during this audit.
Do not paste production secrets into the conversation for verification.
Do not treat recommendations as a substitute for human security approval.

faq.question: What does this skill review?
faq.answer: It reviews command execution, tool permissions, secrets management, WebSocket security, and selected frontend risks.

faq.question: Does it change my code?
faq.answer: No. The skill states that the audit is read-only and that fixes require user approval.

faq.question: Can it find every vulnerability?
faq.answer: No. It is a guided code review checklist, not a full penetration test or automated scanner.

faq.question: Which assistants can use it?
faq.answer: The report lists support for Claude, Codex, and Claude Code.

faq.question: Is it safe with secrets?
faq.answer: The skill instructs the assistant to avoid logging or exposing discovered secrets.

faq.question: When should I use it?
faq.answer: Use it before deployment, after permission changes, or when reviewing command execution and WebSocket features.
